prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene at magic angles and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred single-part prize, with the same three names. What persuades me is the structure of the evidence. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a quantitative, falsifiable statement, namely a vanishing Dirac velocity and flat bands at discrete twist angles, and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity in precisely that structure. Since then many independent groups have reproduced the phases in twisted graphene and in other moire systems, and the knobs are a gate voltage and a twist angle. That is the closing of a theory-experiment loop, and I think it is the discovery that best fits the kind of prize I want to see at the centre of a condensed-matter award. The citation is written around the flat-band platform and the observed correlated phases, and deliberately makes no claim about the pairing mechanism, which is a follow-up question and not part of the discovery. Three members put it first, four ranked it in their top three, and four others name it as an alternative or fallback, so it is the only candidate that is both a first choice for a block of the committee and acceptable to nearly everyone else.
statement.case_against: The weaknesses are real and I have not argued them away. The field is about eight years old and the superconducting pairing mechanism is open. Several colleagues (Danielsson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth) treat age as a discount, and I accept that this is a legitimate maturity standard, even if I judge that reproduction of the phases by many groups meets it. Attribution is the sharper problem. Earlier twisted-bilayer theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto preceded the continuum model, and Yuan Cao and the Dean group's moire experiments sit outside three names. I cannot settle the priority history from the material before us, and I would not want the committee to hide that behind a confident citation. Lastly, B057 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist and the strongest direct expertise behind it, and if the committee concludes that B015 credit cannot be defended, I would accept B057 without reluctance.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock claim is a quantified number that other laboratories check against their own, that a field-opening argument does not automatically outweigh a decisive measured advance, and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes recognised enabling tools and a different platform.
responses.response: This is a fair challenge to my eighth place and it moves me. I ranked clocks low mainly because of the overlap with 2005 and 2012 and because I lack the expertise, and you and Lindroth give a better account than I had: the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct step, with a measured gain from the 1e-15 range to 1e-18 and cross-laboratory frequency-ratio agreement, which is the independent confirmation I ask of any result. I still do not think field-opening is a weaker standard than a measured improvement, but I agree it does not automatically win. Your point on twist-angle disorder is also fair, and it is why I prefer a citation about the existence of the flat-band correlated phases, which many groups reproduce despite that variability, over any quantitative claim. I have raised B057 from the weakest position in my own thinking to my first fallback, and I would vote for it if B015 falters.

responses.point: Pearce observes that the two atomic-physics members both put B057 first, that the condensed-matter disagreement is within the field, and that the choice is honestly one between breadth of agreement and perceived novelty.
responses.response: I accept the deference argument and apply it in both directions: on clocks I weight Lindroth and Kroll above my own view, and on B015 and B053 I would ask you to weight the condensed-matter members, who are three of four for B015 on the first ballot. But breadth of agreement is not my decision rule. Eight rankings measure how few objections there are, not how much was discovered. I use two tests: whether the central result is independently reproduced, and whether theory can explain what was seen. B015 passes the first in many laboratories and the second at the level of flat bands, though not for the pairing. B057 passes both more cleanly. So it comes down to how much weight maturity gets against how much novelty, and I put that weight slightly towards novelty, while saying that your framing of it as a genuine trade-off is correct.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that dropping Mele from a Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan trio is the least defensible cut, that Kane and Mele wrote the paper that started the subject, and that the 2016 topology prize overlaps B053.
responses.response: I concede the Mele point. In round 1 I proposed Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan because the ARPES identification of the 3D phase is the spectroscopic confirmation I value, but a prize that credits Kane for the Z2 invariant and omits Mele misstates the history of the paper. If the committee goes to B053 I would back your Kane, Mele, Molenkamp configuration, with the citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall prediction and its HgTe observation, and accept that Hasan and the 3D branch fall outside. That is also why I would not lead with B053: it is the candidate where the three-name limit forces the most visible omissions, Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang. Your concern about overlap with 2016 is, however, a point for B053 being less new, which helps B015 in my ranking.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B015 first for the simple, analysable flat-band mechanism, says the citation should rest on the platform and not on an unresolved pairing theory, and names B053 as the more mature fallback if the committee wants more consolidation.
responses.response: We agree on the citation, and I have kept the wording about prediction of flat bands and the observed correlated states. On your fallback I would reverse the order. If the committee wants more consolidation than B015 offers, my first fallback now is B057 and not B053, because B057 has no attribution difficulty comparable to the Kane-Mele-Hasan split, while B053 also has an overlap question with 2016. I would add that the priority question around Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto should be handled in the citation text, by naming the quantitative flat-band prediction and the experimental discovery, and not by changing the names. Our unresolved point is whether Yuan Cao should displace a name; under a three-person limit I do not think there is a defensible way to add him without removing Bistritzer, whose continuum model is the prediction itself.

responses.point: Olsson says the 2018 experiment is the original experiment and not a later elegant one, and cautions that the B053 trio with Mele omitted is hard to defend and that the Kane-Mele versus Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang record should be checked before the committee commits.
responses.response: I agree on the original-experiment test, which B015 passes and which counts for B015 in my judgement. On B053, I have changed my own position as I said to Danielsson: Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the defensible trio, not the one I gave in round 1. I share your wish to check the Kane-Mele versus Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang chain before any commitment to B053, since the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal is what Molenkamp's experiment tested. That unresolved allocation is another reason B053 should stay behind B015 and B057 for me. On B015 itself, your point about Yuan Cao is the one I find hardest, and I do not have a clean answer under the limit of three.

responses.point: Johansson moved from circuit QED to lattice clocks, accepted my reservation about a second superconducting-circuit prize soon after 2025, and said he gives Lindroth and Kroll's judgement considerable weight on clocks.
responses.response: Your reasoning on B021 matches mine, and I appreciate that you flagged your own conflict with it; I would not push B021 given the 2025 prize and your and Kroll's declared WACQT ties. Your shift to B057 is a substantive signal because you moved on the merits after reading the others and not because of a vote count. I note that, like me, you list B015 as an alternative, so there is overlap in what we find acceptable. I can accept B057 if the committee prefers, and I would join you in asking that the citation be written around the lattice clock as a measurement instrument, so that it does not reach into the 2005 and 2012 territory.

uncertainties: Whether the priority of the Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction over earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) can be settled; I cannot verify it from the record before me.
Whether Yuan Cao and the Dean group should enter the credit, which the three-person limit makes hard without dropping Bistritzer, MacDonald or Jarillo-Herrero.
Whether eight years of reproduction without an agreed pairing mechanism clears the committee's maturity standard, a judgement on which my colleagues reasonably differ from me.
How far Lemonde, Gill, Hollberg and Ludlow change the B057 credit; I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on this and cannot judge it independently.
Whether a two-part configuration is feasible at all: pairing B015 with B057 or B053 would exceed three people unless one B015 name were dropped, and I do not support that cost.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited candidate, institution or collaborator in B015, B057 or B053. I work on first-principles electronic structure and magnetism, and 2D materials in general, but I have no joint work, funding or supervisory link with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele or Molenkamp. I chaired the 2025 committee, which is not a conflict. I defer to Lindroth and Kroll on atomic clocks and to Johansson and Kroll's own recusal statements on circuit QED.
